## [T3] pipeline/development/arena_closure/output/cluster_reports/c016_report.md

# FCAS Revenue Compression and the Battery Business Case: A Portfolio Review

## The mechanism in plain language

A recurring failure pattern across ARENA's storage and ancillary-services portfolio is what might be called the "first-mover premium decay" problem in Frequency Control Ancillary Services (FCAS) markets. Battery and other fast-response projects have routinely been justified to investors and to ARENA on financial models that assume continuation — or only modest decline — of the high FCAS prices observed in the early years of operation. In practice, those high prices have been a transient artefact of thin markets with few qualified providers. As subsequent batteries enter, prices compress sharply, and the revenue stack that underwrote the original investment thins out from the bottom up. The Hornsdale Power Reserve effect — a single 100 MW battery taking 55% of South Australia's FCAS market and crashing prices by roughly 90% in early 2018 [Networks Renewed/ARENA-DLV-0954-0038] — is the canonical illustration: the same asset that demonstrated FCAS commercial viability simultaneously demonstrated how easily it could be eroded.

This matters disproportionately for ARENA because the Agency's mandate sits at exactly the project stage where this risk is invisible. ARENA funds first-of-kind and early-mover deployments whose business cases lean heavily on services revenues that have not yet been competed away. The cluster contains 59 records from 23 projects across 11 categories — battery storage, hybrid systems, V2G, demand response, pumped hydro, distributed energy resources, system security, even concentrated solar thermal — meaning the mechanism is not a battery-specific quirk but a structural feature of how shallow ancillary-service markets interact with successive waves of ARENA-style demonstration funding.

## The causal pathway

The vulnerability arises from a specific market structure. FCAS markets in the NEM are small in absolute terms — roughly 210–220 MW for regulation and 350–450 MW for contingency [c016/ARENA-DLV-1086-0057] — and the marginal cost of supply from a fast-response battery is essentially zero once the asset exists. A small number of projects can saturate the market, and the next entrant is a price-taker into a clearing price that its own bid drives down. The proximate failure manifests as a step-change between operating year one and year two: revenues that anchored the investment case fall sharply and persistently, not because of asset underperformance but because the market has restructured around the new entrants. Gannawarra Energy Storage System (GESS) is the cleanest empirical example — FCAS revenue collapsed from roughly $500,000/month in its first operating year to roughly $150,000/month in its second, a ~70% reduction with no change in the asset itself [c016/ARENA-DLV-0541-0018, c016/ARENA-DLV-0539-0007].

What distinguishes this mechanism from adjacent ones is the source of the compression. It is not driven primarily by the renewables-penetration effects that raise *requirement* for FCAS (cluster c650), nor by reserved-capacity tradeoffs within an asset (c948), nor by regulatory rule changes (c903) — though all of these can compound it. The core dynamic is endogenous: success of the deployment model creates the conditions under which subsequent deployments cannot replicate the original returns. It is, in effect, a tragedy-of-the-commons in a finite revenue pool, with each new entrant rationally optimising against a price curve that their collective entry destroys.

## Manifestation across the portfolio

The pattern appears at three distinguishable points in the project lifecycle.

**At feasibility and application stage**, it shows up as wide divergence in FCAS price assumptions between applicants. ARENA's own portfolio review noted that some applicants assumed current high FCAS prices would persist while others applied aggressive decay curves [c016/ARENA-DLV-0402-0060]. The AECOM analysis commissioned by ARENA, which modelled exponential decline to 10% of current FCAS prices by 2040, was being used by some applicants (notably the ANU community-battery work [Community Models for Deploying and Operating DER, c016/ARENA-DLV-0597-0046, c016/ARENA-DLV-0401-0048]) but evidently not by others. One LSBS portfolio review explicitly applied a -10% per annum de-escalator [c016/ARENA-DLV-0784-0076], implying that even at the time of review the variance in applicant practice was material. This matters because the bankability gap — projects requiring FCAS revenues but unable to bank them [c016/ARENA-DLV-0254-0016, c016/ARENA-DLV-0556-0009, c016/ARENA-DLV-0651-0041] — has been consistently bridged by ARENA grant funding, transferring the price-trajectory risk implicitly onto the public balance sheet.

**At early-operations stage**, it shows up as the GESS-style year-two surprise. The Wallgrove battery experienced this in a more attenuated form: regulation FCAS revenue declined from $2.3M (H1 2022) to $1.2M (H2 2023), though aggregate revenues across all markets stayed relatively stable as the operator restacked into other streams [TransGrid Wallgrove Battery, c016/ARENA-DLV-0978-0043]. ESCRI/Dalrymple in South Australia reported FCAS forming over 90% of competitive market revenue in its first six months — a concentration that the project itself flagged as a risk for the next wave of batteries [Energy Storage for Commercial Renewable Integration Phase 2, c016/ARENA-DLV-0480-0070, c016/ARENA-DLV-0479-0050]. Even non-battery ancillary-service plays were affected: United Energy's voltage-controlled FCAS trial, designed to monetise its Dynamic Voltage Management System, found that R5M revenues had collapsed across 2017–2020 — Q3 revenues falling from ~$26,600 (2018) to $539 (2020) — to the point where projected revenue fell below the daily maintenance cost threshold [United Energy Voltage Controlled Frequency Regulation System, c016/ARENA-DLV-1030-0041, c016/ARENA-DLV-1030-0045, c016/ARENA-DLV-1030-0050].

**At late or post-deployment stage**, the mechanism manifests as commercial models that simply did not survive contact with the market. The United Energy Low Voltage Battery Trial is the most striking case: by the time the pole-mounted distributed battery fleet was ready for FCAS participation, contingency prices had compressed to the point where the retail partner advised it was no longer economic to register at all [United Energy Low Voltage Battery Trial, c016/ARENA-DLV-1008-0002, c016/ARENA-DLV-1008-0039, c016/ARENA-DLV-1008-0003]. The trial proved technical feasibility but lost the commercial window — a pattern with uncomfortable echoes of merchant generation projects that come online into a saturated market. Similarly, Hornsdale Wind Farm Stage 2 found that the regulation FCAS opportunity for additional wind providers had already been compressed by the entry of HPR and HDWF2 itself [Hornsdale Wind Farm Stage 2 FCAS Trial, c016/ARENA-DLV-0742-0038].

A sub-pattern worth flagging is the **adjacent-market displacement effect**. As FCAS compresses in primary markets, projects look to secondary streams — SRAS, contingency 6-second/60-second/5-minute markets, energy arbitrage, network leasing. Each of these secondary streams is itself thin and subject to the same compression dynamic. The ESCRI BESS turned to contingency FCAS as regulation eroded; GESS registered for contingency markets in its third year only to face Victorian Big Battery competition [Gannawarra/c016/ARENA-DLV-0539-0012]. SRAS was identified as a potential future revenue stream for several projects but assessed as economically unattractive due to competition from less capital-intensive incumbents [c016/ARENA-DLV-0556-0091]. The pattern is thus not "FCAS revenue falls" but rather "each successive ancillary-service revenue pool is competed away in turn", with cycle time accelerating.

## Project-level context

The project context illuminates *why* certain projects bore this risk acutely. GESS, with $22.7M of ARENA funding against a $41.2M project value, was a co-located battery+solar deployment whose merchant exposure was substantial; its operator was sophisticated, and the FCAS revenue collapse was not a planning failure but a market reality the project documented carefully across reporting periods. ESCRI Phase 2, similarly, was a network-adjacent battery (ElectraNet) whose primary value was system-security oriented, but whose competitive market revenues to defray cost depended on the same FCAS pool. The United Energy LV trial is the most cautionary case from a portfolio-design perspective: at $4M ARENA funding into a $14.4M trial whose commercial model rested on retail-partner FCAS participation, the project was structurally vulnerable to the precise mechanism that ultimately materialised, and the cascade of upstream manufacturing/installation delays [event EVT-0002] meant the project entered the FCAS market window after it had effectively closed.

A different lens applies to the feasibility-study projects — EnergyAustralia PHES, Shoalhaven, the ANU community models work. Here, FCAS compression entered the projects as a *finding* rather than a project-level failure: studies that initially assumed FCAS as a meaningful revenue line revised that assumption downward during the analysis itself, with consequences for the apparent commercial viability of the underlying technology [c016/ARENA-DLV-0506-0045, c016/ARENA-DLV-0899-0083]. In several cases this contributed to projects not progressing to deployment. From a portfolio-risk standpoint, this is arguably a healthier outcome: the feasibility funding surfaced the vulnerability before deployment capital was committed.

## Event-level context

The event-sibling structure shows that FCAS compression rarely sits alone. In the Ballarat BESS project, the cluster record on FCAS uncertainty sits alongside sibling records [c650/ARENA-DLV-0332-0056, c650/ARENA-DLV-0334-0032] showing that high renewables penetration was simultaneously suppressing both energy and FCAS prices — a compounding rather than offsetting dynamic. In the United Energy LV trial, the FCAS-failure record sits in an event with cascading delay records [c648/ARENA-DLV-1005-0086, c565/ARENA-DLV-1005-0101] and a regulatory-rule-change record [c903/ARENA-DLV-1008-0032]: the proximate cause of commercial failure was FCAS compression, but the underlying vulnerability was a project schedule that exhausted the commercial window. The Rheem hot-water VPP shows FCAS dilution from new residential battery entrants paired with regulatory uncertainty over MASS rules [c682/ARENA-DLV-1378-0019] — the two risks reinforce each other because rule changes can themselves accelerate competitive entry. Reading across these event clusters, the mechanism is best understood as a *vulnerability* that is triggered or amplified by adjacent failures — schedule slippage, regulatory shifts, renewables-driven energy-price suppression — rather than as a free-standing failure mode.

## Mitigations observed

Several mitigation strategies appear across the records, with varying success.

*Conservative price assumptions in evaluation*. The -10% de-escalator practice [c016/ARENA-DLV-0784-0076] and the AECOM exponential-decline curve [c016/ARENA-DLV-0597-0046] represent attempts to discipline applicant projections. Implementation appears uneven across the portfolio.

*Revenue stacking and rotation*. Wallgrove's relatively stable aggregate revenues despite regulation FCAS decline [c016/ARENA-DLV-0978-0043] suggest that operators with mature trading capability can rotate between revenue streams, partially offsetting compression in any single one. This requires sophisticated optimisation infrastructure — the ESCRI sibling records [event EVT-0019] note that AGL was still developing arbitrage-vs-FCAS optimisation modules as five-minute settlement approached.

*Network-service contracting*. Several records emphasise that network-benefit revenues, where contractable on long-term terms, provide a hedge against merchant FCAS volatility — though the ARENA review noted that networks themselves are uncertain about their ability to negotiate or sustain such leases [c016/ARENA-DLV-0402-0074]. This is the implicit logic behind ESCRI and Wallgrove's network-host structures.

*Direct facilitation*. The portfolio-level review [c016/ARENA-DLV-0556-0047] candidly observes that most grid-scale BESS to date has required direct government facilitation. This is itself a mitigation, but one that does not scale.

*Hedging product development*. The Renewable Energy Hub Marketplace project [c016/ARENA-DLV-0856-0046] is notable as a project that takes FCAS compression as a given and attempts to build the financial-product infrastructure (hedge contracts) that would let battery operators monetise firming and arbitrage revenues more reliably. This is the most structurally responsive mitigation in the corpus — addressing the underlying bankability problem rather than the symptom.

## Implications for portfolio decisions

For a portfolio manager, three concrete implications follow.

**At funding-decision time**, FCAS revenue assumptions in applicant business cases should be treated as a primary risk parameter, not a secondary financial input. A standardised stress-test — for example, applying the AECOM-style decline curve and asking whether the project remains viable — would quickly separate projects whose case is robust from those that are essentially a bet that the applicant will be early enough to capture the compression premium. Where the latter is the case, that should be made explicit. The corpus suggests that ARENA has implicitly been funding compression-premium bets without always pricing them as such.

**At milestone-review time**, year-one FCAS performance is a leading indicator, not a result. Strong year-one numbers should trigger heightened scrutiny of year-two projections rather than reassurance, because year-one returns reflect the market state *before* the funded project (and its successors in the pipeline) have changed it. The GESS reporting cadence [event EVT-0004, event EVT-0008] is a model: granular tracking of FCAS revenue evolution by half-year, with explicit attribution to market-share and competitor-entry dynamics.

**At handover and knowledge-sharing time**, the corpus would benefit from a standardised retrospective on the gap between business-case FCAS revenue and realised FCAS revenue, with attribution between price compression, dispatch performance, and market-design changes. Several projects produce this implicitly; few produce it in a comparable form.

**At programme design level**, ARENA may want to consider whether sequential funding of similar batteries into the same FCAS market constitutes — viewed from outside — a form of subsidised cannibalisation. If the public benefit of project N+1 is partly offset by the revenue erosion it imposes on already-funded projects 1 through N, the marginal-benefit calculation is not what it appears.

## Open questions and evidence gaps

The corpus is rich on the *symptom* but thin on several aspects of the underlying dynamic.

First, there is essentially no empirical work in the corpus on the *floor* of FCAS price compression — at what level prices stabilise once the market is saturated, and whether that floor reflects long-run marginal cost of provision or some other equilibrium. The ANU community-battery projects use the AECOM decline-to-10% curve, but the empirical basis for that floor is unclear.

Second, the interaction between FCAS compression and the introduction of Primary Frequency Response, the 1-second/2-second contingency markets, and broader frequency-control rule reforms is acknowledged [c016/ARENA-DLV-0332-0060, c016/ARENA-DLV-0332-0061] but not quantified. Rule changes can both compress (by mandating provision) and expand (by creating new product markets) the available revenue pool; the corpus does not resolve which dominates.

Third, the V2G records [c016/ARENA-DLV-0031-0012, c016/ARENA-DLV-0031-0037, c016/ARENA-DLV-0950-0097] anticipate massive future EV-driven FCAS supply but contain no empirical data on whether this is materialising — it is forward-looking concern rather than observed phenomenon.

Fourth, the corpus contains very little on whether projects that survived FCAS compression did so through superior trading, hardware capability (e.g. faster response), site-specific advantages, or simply scale — i.e. what differentiates resilient from fragile FCAS revenue strategies. Wallgrove's relative stability hints at trading sophistication but is not isolated as a causal factor.

Filling these gaps — in particular through a coordinated cross-project retrospective on realised vs. projected FCAS revenues, indexed to market-share and competitor-entry timelines — would substantially sharpen the portfolio's ability to evaluate the next wave of storage and ancillary-service applications.

## [T3] pipeline/development/arena_closure/output/cluster_reports/c1074_report.md

# Conservative Third-Party Engineering Bias Toward Over-Specification

## A pattern of asymmetric incentives at the technical-advisory layer

Across ARENA's portfolio, there is a recurring failure mode that lives not in the technology being funded, nor in the proponent organisation, but in the *advisory layer* between them — the independent engineers, certification consultants, transmission network service providers (TNSPs), specifying authorities, and equipment vendors whose sign-off is required to move a project forward. The mechanism is straightforward and economically rational: these third parties bear concentrated downside risk if a design they signed off on fails in the field, but capture none of the upside if the design is optimised. The rational response is to over-specify — to apply the most conservative interpretation of every standard, to assume the worst plausible loading or operating condition, to default to the most familiar (and typically heaviest, largest, costliest) configuration. The proponent absorbs the resulting cost inflation, sometimes catastrophically.

This archetype appears in seven distinct projects spanning five ARENA categories — battery storage, concentrated solar thermal, solar PV, system security, and renewables for industry. That breadth is itself a finding: this is not a quirk of one technology family or one regulatory regime. It is a structural feature of how technical risk is allocated whenever a novel or non-standard design must pass through an established advisory function. For a portfolio whose mandate is precisely to fund the novel and non-standard, the mechanism is endemic rather than incidental.

## The causal pathway

The vulnerability arises wherever three conditions coincide. First, a proponent is pursuing a design that diverges — sometimes mildly, sometimes radically — from incumbent practice. Second, that design must be validated, certified, connected, or specified by an independent technical party whose professional liability attaches to the sign-off. Third, the standards or norms available to that party were calibrated against incumbent technology and offer no defensible margin for optimisation toward the new design.

Under these conditions, the third party faces a sharply asymmetric payoff: a conservative recommendation produces no career or commercial reward but eliminates liability; an optimised recommendation produces no fee uplift but creates a defensible target if anything goes wrong later. The proximate failure is over-specification — heavier structures, larger transformers, oversized boilers, tighter harmonic allocations, evaporator tubes built to superheater spec — and the cost shows up on the proponent's capex line.

What distinguishes this mechanism from adjacent ones is important. It is *not* the same as risk-averse adoption delay (cluster c536), where the conservatism slows or blocks the decision to adopt at all; here the project proceeds, but with a fattened cost base. It is *not* the same as inadequate measurement infrastructure (c894), though the two often co-occur — measurement gaps *enable* the conservative bias by removing the empirical basis for arguing against it. And it is not generic engineering conservatism: it is specifically conservatism produced by *misaligned incentives at the advisory interface*, which means the mitigation set is institutional rather than technical.

## Manifestation across the portfolio

The clearest articulation comes from the 5B Maverick project [c1074/ARENA-DLV-1092-0020], where the proponent named the mechanism in essentially economic terms: independent wind tunnel consultants have no upside for optimisation and material downside for any field failure traceable to deviation from norms. The 5B case is also the most fully documented at event level. The wind certification difficulty was compounded by measurement infrastructure designed for high-rise buildings rather than ground-mounted low-load PV arrays [ARENA-DLV-1092-0021], which produced a poor signal-to-noise ratio that *itself* fed back into conservative load assumptions — when the measurement is noisy, the defensible response is to take the upper envelope. 5B's workaround was a multi-laboratory round robin to triangulate true loads [ARENA-DLV-0195-0058], described as slow and expensive. The same event cluster captures the broader problem of asking incumbent-trained engineers to assess novel geometries [ARENA-DLV-0195-0057].

In the network and grid-connection space, the AGL Liddell BESS project [Liddell Large Scale Battery] shows the mechanism operating through the regulatory-standards interface rather than the consultancy interface. The TNSP applied its NER-regulated asset standards to a privately owned connection substation [c1074/ARENA-DLV-1105-0017], inflating footprint and cost, and was unwilling to deviate. A sibling record [ARENA-DLV-1105-0018] shows the same pattern producing a specific equipment-level penalty: oversized current transformers were specified instead of relying on modern relay algorithms to handle CT saturation, delaying switchboard manufacture. This is the same archetype with different actors — the TNSP plays the role the wind consultant plays for 5B, and the asymmetry is identical: deviating from regulated asset standards exposes the TNSP to liability with no offsetting reward.

In concentrated solar thermal, the Collinsville hybrid project [Conversion of Coal to Hybrid Solar Thermal/Gas] shows the mechanism inside the EPC supply chain. The vendor (Novatec) specified evaporator tubes to the same standard as superheater tubes [c1074/ARENA-DLV-1429-0004], which contributed materially to a solar field cost overrun. The event context is sobering: the EPC tender came in 84% above the May 2013 budget estimate [ARENA-DLV-1428-0003], with currency moves explaining roughly 16.5% [ARENA-DLV-1428-0004] and the residual driven by solar-field-specific cost inflation [ARENA-DLV-1428-0005]. Over-specification was one of several contributors, but it sat inside a stack that ultimately killed project feasibility. The same project's design-proliferation problem [ARENA-DLV-1428-0006] is in fact the same evaporator-tube issue viewed through a different cluster lens, which is itself instructive — over-specification and design proliferation tend to coincide because conservative spec choices propagate as bespoke variants.

The CSIRO heliostat R&D project [Novel Concepts for Low Cost Small Heliostats] reveals a slightly different manifestation: site-specific uncertainty drives conservative costings and safety factors as a *default* posture pending full site characterisation [c1074/ARENA-DLV-1310-0022]. The event sibling [ARENA-DLV-1310-0032] explains why this becomes structural: full geotechnical and wind characterisation is expensive and impractical at early project stages, so conservative assumptions are locked into commercial offers. The advisor's incentive asymmetry here is reinforced by genuine information scarcity.

In system security, the Wollongong harmonic distortion project [Impact and Management of Harmonic Distortion] surfaces the mechanism at the regulatory-modelling layer [c1074/ARENA-DLV-1009-0011]: harmonic allocations to renewable generators appear systematically too stringent, with the empirical evidence being that distortion levels have *fallen* despite increased connection of harmonic sources. The event context [ARENA-DLV-1009-0012] points to modelling practices being inaccurate as well as overly stringent — a double penalty for renewable generators required to invest in mitigation that the network does not actually need.

The remaining two records show the archetype in different guises. The Renewable Energy for Process Heat study [c1074/ARENA-DLV-0869-0012] documents a sales-side variant: conventional boiler quotes are oversized for rare peaks, and when heat pump alternatives are required to match nameplate boiler capacity, the comparison is structurally biased against the renewable option. United Energy's peak-demand-deferral work [c1074/ARENA-DLV-0879-0094] is the mildest case in the cluster — really a methodological caution about not over-specifying storage deployment in high-growth areas — but it belongs because the same logic is at play: defaulting to a conservative storage sizing assumption rather than tuning to actual local growth rates produces over-specification.

## Sub-patterns

Three sub-patterns are visible. The first is *certification-interface* over-specification (5B Maverick, Collinsville evaporator tubes, heliostat safety factors) — independent engineers signing off on novel hardware. The second is *regulatory-asset* over-specification (Liddell TNSP standards, harmonic allocations) — established network operators applying incumbent rules to novel connections. The third is *commercial-comparison* over-specification (process heat boiler sizing) — incumbent quoting practices that disadvantage renewable alternatives even before formal evaluation begins. All three share the underlying asymmetry, but the leverage points for mitigation differ.

## Mitigation patterns observed

The corpus is thinner on mitigations than on the mechanism itself, which is telling. 5B's multi-laboratory round-robin [ARENA-DLV-0195-0058] is the clearest worked example: when no single advisor can be pushed off the conservative envelope, run several in parallel to characterise the envelope itself. It works but is slow and expensive. The Wollongong harmonics project implicitly proposes a different mitigation: empirical recalibration of the allocation methodology against observed network behaviour, on the basis that the underlying modelling is wrong and not merely cautious. The heliostat project points toward earlier and cheaper site characterisation as a way to collapse the uncertainty that conservative assumptions are filling.

What is conspicuously absent is any record of an effective renegotiation of the *liability allocation* itself — i.e., a contractual or institutional arrangement under which the third party is rewarded for, or at least not penalised for, optimisation. This is the underlying economic problem and the corpus suggests it is being routed around rather than solved.

## Project-level context

The funding scale across the cluster spans three orders of magnitude, from the $146k Wollongong harmonics study to the $694m Liddell BESS, and the mechanism appears at every scale. That is itself important: this is not a small-project problem driven by lean engineering teams nor a large-project problem driven by bureaucratic inertia. It is invariant to scale because it is invariant to the asymmetry that produces it.

Two project-level observations sharpen the picture. First, the projects where the mechanism produced the most material damage — Collinsville (project ultimately not feasible) and Liddell (live cost and schedule impact on a $694m build) — are projects where the third-party advisor sat on the *critical path* of capex commitment, not in an advisory side-channel. The leverage of the conservative bias scales with how directly the advisor's sign-off translates into procurement. Second, R&D-stage projects (heliostats, harmonics) tend to surface the mechanism as a *characterised problem* rather than a realised cost — they are doing the diagnostic work that deployment-stage projects pay for in capex.

## Implications for portfolio decisions

At funding-decision time, the relevant due-diligence question is not "does this design work" but "which third parties must sign off on this design, and what are their incentive structures." Projects that route around incumbent advisory infrastructure (in-house certification, vendor-integrated testing, novel measurement chains) carry a different risk profile than projects that depend on a TNSP, an independent engineer, or a standards body whose mandate predates the technology. For a portfolio whose value proposition is novelty, the latter category should expect a conservative-bias premium baked into capex estimates, and proponents who have not budgeted for it are under-budgeted.

At milestone-review time, the diagnostic signal is cost variance concentrated in line items signed off by independent advisors rather than by the proponent's engineers. The Collinsville solar field overrun [Conversion of Coal to Hybrid Solar Thermal/Gas] and the Liddell substation footprint inflation [AGL Liddell] are textbook examples — overruns that look like generic cost inflation but on inspection trace to specific specification choices made by parties outside the proponent's control. Reviewers should ask whether overruns are concentrated at advisory interfaces.

At handover and knowledge-capture time, the most valuable artefacts are not the final designs but the *deltas* between proponent-preferred and advisor-required specifications, with cost attached. These deltas are the empirical basis for any future renegotiation of standards and allocation methodologies. ARENA's portfolio is in a privileged position to assemble this evidence base across multiple projects and technologies, and the harmonics project [Impact and Management of Harmonic Distortion] is a model for what that empirical recalibration looks like.

A portfolio-level intervention worth considering is convening standards bodies, TNSPs, and certification consultants around specific technology-class evidence packages — wind loading on ground-mount PV, harmonic allocation under high inverter penetration, BESS connection asset standards — to update norms against accumulated field evidence. This is the only mitigation that addresses the mechanism at root rather than working around it.

## Open questions and evidence gaps

The corpus tells us the mechanism exists, where it appears, and roughly what it costs in specific cases. It does not tell us several things that would matter for prioritisation. We do not have a quantified distribution of conservative-bias premium by technology class — anecdotally Collinsville lost 84% to budget but we cannot decompose how much was conservative bias versus currency, scope change, or genuine market price movement. We do not have evidence on whether the bias is increasing or decreasing as renewable technologies mature; the harmonics evidence suggests allocations are still calibrated to old assumptions, but we have no comparable longitudinal data for wind loading, grid connection, or thermal specifications. We have almost no evidence on *successful* renegotiations of advisory liability — cases where a third party was persuaded or contractually structured into supporting an optimised design — which is precisely the evidence needed to design a portfolio-level mitigation. And we have no clear picture of whether Australian advisory practice is more or less conservative than international comparators; the harmonics project hints at this through Dutch, Estonian, and Irish data but does not extend the comparison to other technical domains.

Filling these gaps would not require new projects so much as more structured post-project review of the advisory-interface delta in completed builds. That artefact, assembled across the portfolio, is the substrate on which a structural rather than project-by-project response to this archetype could be built.

## [T3] pipeline/development/arena_closure/output/parent_reports/p18_report.md

# Coupled-Objective Trade-off (p18): When Two Goals Share One Knob

## 1. Framing

A coupled-objective trade-off is the failure pattern that emerges when two performance objectives share a structural coupling such that improving one necessarily degrades the other. It is not an engineering oversight to be designed away; it is a binding constraint inherited from physics, market architecture, contract structure, or system topology. In the ARENA portfolio, this archetype shows up when a single asset is asked to deliver two services that compete for the same finite resource — capacity headroom, electrical current, photons, thermal flux, reactor residence time, regulator attention, customer trust — and where the optimisation frontier between them is convex enough that no single operating point is dominant.

The archetype matters for a renewables-investment portfolio because it sits underneath many of the apparent disappointments of demonstration projects: a wind farm's FCAS trial earning less than the energy it curtails to deliver the service<sup>1,2</sup>, a grid-forming battery whose inertial response weakens precisely as it earns more from energy arbitrage<sup>3,4</sup>, a tandem solar cell whose top sub-cell improvements never translate into module gains because the bottom sub-cell limits current<sup>5</sup>. In each case the project did what was technically asked of it, but the headline metric fell short because the engineering or market structure forced a compromise the business case had not internalised.

The evidence base spans 393 records across 153 projects in 17 ARENA categories, with project years from 2010 to 2025 and publish dates from 2012 to 2026. The 24 constituent clusters cover physical-engineering trade-offs (FCAS headroom vs energy output, photon absorption vs voltage in tandems, kinetic vs thermodynamic optima in chemistry), system-architectural ones (reactive vs real power in inverters, ancillary reservation vs market dispatch), and human/regulatory ones (granularity vs simplicity in tariff design, accuracy vs accessibility in compensation). The breadth itself is informative: where so many distinct technical communities independently rediscover the same shape of problem, the underlying mechanism is structural rather than circumstantial.

## 2. The Mechanism at the Parent Level

The unifying causal pathway can be stated compactly. A system possesses a single binding resource — call it R — that is required for two distinct objectives, A and B. The total demand for R from A and B exceeds the available R at the operating points where both A and B are most valuable. The system is therefore on the Pareto frontier between A and B, and any choice of operating point sacrifices some quantity of one for the other. Crucially, the trade-off is *not* fixable by better engineering of A or B in isolation, because the constraint is on R, not on the conversion of R into A or B.

The shape of R varies by sub-pattern. In FCAS-from-renewables, R is the headroom between current output and maximum available power<sup>1,2,6</sup>. In grid-forming inverters, R is rated kVA and overcurrent margin<sup>4,7</sup>. In tandem solar cells, R is the photon flux through each spectral band, allocated by sub-cell bandgap<sup>5,8</sup>. In ammonia synthesis, R is reactor temperature, which sets both kinetic rate and equilibrium yield in opposing directions<sup>9</sup>. In dynamic network tariff design, R is the regulator's attention and consumer comprehension budget<sup>10,11</sup>.

Where the mechanism depends on time-variant context, the dependencies are real but not always destabilising. Market-rule-based trade-offs (FCAS vs energy co-optimisation) shifted with the introduction of five-minute settlement and changing FCAS market design from 2017 onward. Contract-based trade-offs (RERT availability vs FCAS bidding) reflected the specific NER 3.20.3(j) interpretation operative in 2017–2018<sup>12</sup>. Physical trade-offs in semiconductors and reactor chemistry are time-invariant. The synthesis below names where the trade-off is binding under any plausible future state versus where it is artefact of a particular regulatory or market epoch.

## 3. Sub-Patterns: How the Coupled-Objective Trade-off Manifests

The 24 clusters group naturally into six sub-patterns of expression, each illuminating a different setting where two valued objectives must share one resource.

### 3.1 Headroom-as-resource: ancillary services from energy-bound assets

The largest and most operationally consequential sub-pattern in the corpus involves variable renewable generators and battery storage attempting to provide raise-direction frequency services while also maximising energy revenue. The constituent clusters [c534] and [c948] each describe the same coupling from different angles: raise FCAS requires headroom between current output and capacity, and that headroom is the very thing that energy dispatch consumes.

The Hornsdale Wind Farm 2 FCAS trial provides the canonical evidence base. Average curtailment to provide raise regulation FCAS was 18.7 MW against an average dispatch of only 12.4 MW<sup>1</sup>; the trial earned $24,000 in FCAS revenue against $83,000 of curtailed energy plus LGC value<sup>13</sup>; and 11% of dispatch intervals saw the wind farm stranded outside its FCAS trapezium because its forecast output drifted across the enablement boundary<sup>2</sup>. Musselroe Wind Farm replicated the structural finding, spending only 25–30% of its time within the theoretical generating boundary required for FCAS participation<sup>14</sup>.

The trade-off generalises beyond wind. Lake Bonney BESS achieved 88% enablement in Raise 6 Seconds during high-price intervals but only 24–29% in Raise Regulation, because regulation requires sustained energy throughput that competes with the contingency reserve<sup>15</sup>. The Wallgrove Battery's 50 MW nameplate becomes 24 MW for energy and regulating raise after 26 MW of contingency-raise headroom is reserved<sup>16,17</sup>. In grid-forming batteries the same headroom logic applies to inertia: as the active power setpoint approaches 1 pu, the inertial response diminishes because there is insufficient capacity for a complete response<sup>3,18</sup>. The Liddell BESS was therefore deliberately oversized and operated at 86% of maximum capacity to reserve overcurrent for inertial response<sup>19</sup>.

Sibling event evidence makes clear that this headroom trade-off interacts with adjacent failure modes — inverter current ceilings<sup>20</sup>, plant-controller minimum enablement floors<sup>21,22</sup>, and the forecast-skill ceiling that determines whether headroom can be offered with confidence<sup>23</sup>. The trade-off is structural; the *severity* depends on forecast quality, market design, and contract structure.

### 3.2 Photon and current allocation: the multi-junction PV trade-off

In tandem and multi-junction photovoltaic devices, the binding resource is the solar spectrum, which can be split between sub-cells in only one way at a time. Cluster [c1141] (sub-optimal component constrains whole-system performance) and cluster [c1136] (electrical vs optical in interlayers) capture this from the device-architecture perspective; cluster [c966] (incompatible processing conditions) captures it from the manufacturing perspective.

In ACAP's GaAs/Si four-terminal tandem, silicon cell efficiency dropped from 20.3% standalone to 3.75% in tandem because higher-energy photons were absorbed in the GaAs layer and parasitic losses in the GaAs rear reflector reduced silicon current from 40.2 to 8.3 mA/cm²<sup>5</sup>. In a three-junction InGaP/GaAs/Si Smart Stack, the silicon bottom cell limited overall performance through optical losses<sup>8</sup>. UNSW's GaAsP/SiGe project found the SiGe bottom cell current was the binding constraint, and recommended prioritising bottom-cell current over top-cell improvements because of the current-matching requirement of two-terminal tandems<sup>24</sup>.

The same trade-off appears in interlayer design. Transparent conducting oxides such as ITO improve electrical conductivity but cause parasitic absorption in the red wavelengths<sup>25,26</sup>; introducing conductive metals or particles into transparent contact adhesives raises conductivity but degrades transparency<sup>27</sup>. CdS as an electron transport layer has been used in high-efficiency antimony selenide cells but causes parasitic absorption that reduces light reaching the absorber<sup>28</sup>. The optical-electrical coupling means a single material cannot simultaneously be a perfect conductor and a perfect window.

Manufacturing integration sharpens the trade-off further. Hydrogenation processes that improve cell efficiency cause copper contacts to peel from silicon because of thermal expansion mismatch<sup>29</sup>; high-temperature firing required for screen-printed silver contacts degrades polysilicon passivation contacts<sup>30</sup>; black silicon textures that minimise reflection are incompatible with standard metal contact processes, forcing the industry to deploy "grey silicon" with moderate reflectance instead<sup>31,32</sup>. Each integration step asks two layers or two processes to satisfy mutually incompatible requirements through a single fabrication sequence.

### 3.3 Kinetics versus thermodynamics in chemical processes

Cluster [c708] gathers cases where reaction kinetics demand operating conditions that conflict with thermodynamic optima. The mechanism is fundamental: many industrially important reactions are exothermic with negative entropy change, so equilibrium yield is favoured at low temperature and high pressure, while reaction rate is favoured at high temperature.

Ammonia synthesis is the textbook case. CSIRO's hydrogen-to-ammonia project documented that the exothermic reaction is thermodynamically favoured at low temperature but slow kinetics force operation at 400–500°C, where equilibrium yield falls; at 450°C equilibrium ammonia content drops from 22% at 150 bar to 6.5% at 30 bar<sup>9,33</sup>. Calix's ZESTY direct-reduced-iron process exhibits the same pattern: the H₂-iron oxide reaction is endothermic, so complete substitution of methane with hydrogen requires additional heating that the existing CO-iron oxide reaction would otherwise provide<sup>34</sup>. Cavendish's ammonia cracking work notes that decomposition is endothermic and consumes 35% of the hydrogen's usable energy content<sup>35</sup>; in-situ cracking on the SOFC anode creates thermal gradients that stress materials<sup>36</sup>.

The trade-off extends to receiver design. Central tower CSP receivers achieve only ~90% efficiency because of peak flux limits imposed by molten salt and materials constraints<sup>37</sup>. Pursuing supercritical CO₂ Brayton cycles above 700°C raises capital cost of thermal storage<sup>38</sup>. In phosphorus removal from end-of-life PV silicon, vacuum evaporation removed 70–90% of phosphorus but with proportional silicon loss — only 50% of initial silicon mass was recoverable at 10⁻³ atm<sup>39</sup>.

These trade-offs are time-invariant. They will bind any future project with the same chemistry, regardless of market or regulatory context.

### 3.4 Reactive-real power and inverter capacity allocation

Cluster [c543] and the related clusters [c1107] and [c1181] address a coupling specific to inverter-based resources: the inverter's apparent-power capacity is shared between active and reactive power, and reactive-power dispatch to manage voltage simultaneously consumes thermal headroom and current capacity needed for active power.

The University of Melbourne's PV-rich distribution networks study established the mechanism quantitatively: aggregate Volt-var absorption at HV feeder heads can violate transmission-distribution power factor limits<sup>40</sup>, while at lower voltages the reactive absorption increases conductor and transformer currents enough that low-capacity LV transformers become overloaded at PV penetration levels well below those that would constrain a Volt-var-free network<sup>41,42</sup>. AGL's VPP in South Australia found that high local voltage triggered reactive power responses that limited active power available for FCAS; during a large dispatch, site voltages above 250 V curtailed real power output<sup>43,44</sup>. At Mortlake, enabling reactive power prioritisation during current limiting improved reactive output but reduced active output, and the connection assessment team turned the mode off<sup>45</sup>.

Tesla's SA VPP made the binding nature of the trade-off explicit at device level: the most aggressive Volt-var curve required up to 100% of Powerwall inverter output, effectively pausing all other inverter functions including self-consumption, FCAS, and inertia services<sup>46,47</sup>. Hornsdale Power Reserve Expansion noted that the H constant chosen for inertia provision was a compromise — higher inertia raised reactive current rise and settling times beyond NER limits<sup>48</sup>. Grid-forming inverter operation at very low voltage references can deliver nominal power only by violating thermal limits<sup>49</sup>.

### 3.5 Reserved-capacity opportunity cost and value-stream stacking

Cluster [c948] in its commercial expression and clusters [c985] and [c1539] capture trade-offs where the binding constraint is not physical capacity but contractual or market-architectural exclusion. A battery cannot simultaneously bid into the energy market and reserve the same MWh for contingency raise<sup>50</sup>. A demand-response provider under a RERT contract was prohibited (in 2017–2018, given AEMO's interpretation) from bidding the same load into FCAS markets during ITT windows; a seven-day ITT could erode 60 hours of FCAS revenue<sup>12,51</sup>. The Ballarat BESS faced a precautionary 75% SoC cap that drove availability from a potential 98.92% down to 91.05%<sup>52</sup>. Wallgrove Battery operators bid availability out of the market during market suspension to avoid continuous dispatch eroding their stored energy<sup>53</sup>.

The same mechanism appears in V2G trials. Optimising EV charging to minimise marginal emissions raises financial cost relative to convenience charging<sup>54</sup>; day-ahead and real-time market participation are mutually exclusive when both require bulk energy shifting<sup>55</sup>. Project Symphony confirmed that each DER asset can only be controlled for one market service at a time, even when the underlying facility could deliver multiple<sup>56</sup>.

This sub-pattern is partly time-variant: market-rule reform can change which combinations are permissible. The 2024 ARENA Vehicle-to-Grid insights report observed that V2G was not legally allowed to bid into raise regulation FCAS during the REVS trial because of battery wear concerns<sup>57</sup> — a constraint whose rationale (cycling cost) is partly physical and partly contractual.

### 3.6 Stakeholder-utility and regulatory-design trade-offs

Clusters [c1539], [c1104], [c1370], and [c1570] extend the mechanism to design trade-offs in markets, regulatory frameworks, and customer-facing systems. Here the binding resource is comprehensibility, administrative capacity, or stakeholder utility itself.

The ANU machine-learning solar forecasting project found that utilities for different market participants are in direct competition: a single performance measure cannot satisfy generators, networks, and system operators simultaneously<sup>58</sup>. A market-operator-optimal forecast minimises maximum deviation, while a generator-optimal forecast minimises mean error<sup>59</sup>. Project Edith documented the same shape of problem in dynamic network pricing: highly localised dynamic prices reflect physical conditions accurately but fragment the customer experience, while zonally averaged tariffs are accessible but obscure local scarcity<sup>10,60</sup>. Targeted rollouts addressing fairness concerns sacrifice the broader incentive value of full-network signals<sup>11</sup>. The DEIP CER Data Exchange co-design workshop noted that documenting data-sharing arrangements in a guidance note offers flexibility but weak enforcement, while NER prescription gives certainty but resists timely amendment<sup>61</sup>.

Customer compensation in DOE-style schemes faces the same shape: an overly complex compensation system erodes user trust through poor experience, while an overly simplified one erodes trust through inaccuracy<sup>62</sup>. The Advisian wind/solar forecasting project found that biasing forecasts to assist frequency stabilisation conflicts with the project objective of pure forecast accuracy<sup>63</sup>.

## 4. Cross-Cutting Observations

Three patterns emerge when the sub-patterns are read together.

**The trade-off frontier is rarely linear, and the steepness of the frontier determines whether the project is investible.** In FCAS-from-wind, the curtailment-to-FCAS ratio at Hornsdale was approximately 1.5:1 in MW terms (18.7 MW curtailment for 12.4 MW dispatch capacity)<sup>1</sup>, and the resulting net loss was the predictable consequence of a steep frontier rather than a project failure. In tandem solar, the current-matching constraint creates a particularly punishing frontier where a 10% mismatch between sub-cells can cost more than 10% of total efficiency<sup>5</sup>. In ammonia synthesis, the equilibrium-vs-rate frontier is steep enough that conventional Haber-Bosch's recycle-loop architecture exists precisely because no single-pass operating point is economic<sup>33</sup>. Steepness, not the existence of the trade-off, is the investible variable.

**Trade-offs propagate into adjacent failure modes when treated as if they were engineering oversights.** The event-sibling evidence shows this clearly. When FCAS-trapezium stranding (a direct expression of the headroom trade-off) is treated as a control architecture issue, plant-controller minimum-enablement floors become a separate failure mode at clusters [c581]<sup>21,22</sup>. When inverter current ceilings (a direct expression of the kVA trade-off) are treated as an inverter design issue rather than a trade-off, they appear as their own failure mode under inverter-based-resource grid interaction<sup>20</sup>. The temptation to engineer around a structural trade-off generally moves the failure to an adjacent surface rather than eliminating it.

**The salience of certain sub-patterns has shifted with technology and market state.** The FCAS-headroom sub-pattern was acutely salient in 2017–2018 when the Hornsdale, Musselroe, ESCRI and Lake Bonney trials were running, and remains salient today, but the *quantitative* parameters have shifted: GFM batteries with VMM now provide synthetic inertia using headroom that is partly compensated by separate procurement<sup>48</sup>; the 5-minute settlement transition (2021) altered the energy-vs-FCAS arbitrage<sup>15</sup>. By contrast, the kinetics-vs-thermodynamics sub-pattern in ammonia and DRI chemistry is essentially unchanged across the 2018–2025 period — Calix in 2024 faces the same H₂-iron-oxide endothermicity constraint that CSIRO articulated in 2018<sup>34,9</sup>. The PV multi-junction sub-pattern shows steady improvement at the Pareto frontier (record efficiencies climb) without changing the underlying coupling.

## 5. Project- and Event-Level Context

Several projects in the corpus illustrate that multiple sub-patterns of this archetype can coexist within a single asset. Hornsdale Power Reserve Expansion shows the headroom trade-off (inertia vs energy)<sup>3,18</sup>, the inverter-capacity trade-off (real vs reactive in the H-constant tuning)<sup>48</sup>, and the modular-versus-fixed scalability trade-off in synchronous condenser comparison<sup>64</sup>. Musselroe Wind Farm shows headroom trade-off, plant-controller floor effects<sup>22</sup>, and reactive-vs-active trapezium constraints<sup>14</sup>. Lake Bonney BESS shows reservation-for-FCAS opportunity cost<sup>15</sup>, AEMO-imposed islanding constraints reducing the operating envelope<sup>65</sup>, and warranty-throughput-as-binding-constraint reducing arbitrage<sup>66</sup>.

The event-sibling structure reveals that when the coupled-objective trade-off is the assigned parent, the most common adjacent failure modes are: control architecture and control-loop failure (when plant controllers cannot navigate the trade-off in real time), inverter-based-resource grid-interaction failure (when the trade-off interacts with weak-grid dynamics), price-signal distortion (when the trade-off is mediated by a market price that does not reflect the physical cost), and forecast-skill ceiling (when the trade-off depends on operating data that is itself uncertain). This co-location is informative for portfolio management: a project flagged for coupled-objective trade-off risk is statistically more likely to encounter one of these adjacent modes during commissioning or early operation.

## 6. Temporal Trajectory

The evidence dates split into three eras. The 2010–2014 records are dominated by physical-trade-off cases in solar PV materials, CSP receiver design, and early FCAS thinking. The 2017–2021 records are dominated by FCAS, inverter, and DER trade-offs as the National Electricity Market began absorbing variable renewables and storage at scale. The 2022–2025 records add hydrogen, iron-and-steel chemistry, and dynamic-tariff/regulatory design trade-offs, plus advanced inverter (GFM) trade-offs.

The mechanism class is not weakening over time. If anything, it is becoming more visible because the portfolio is increasingly tackling problems whose value proposition depends on co-optimisation. A 2012 PV-cell project could in principle be evaluated as a single-objective efficiency problem; a 2024 GFM battery project must be evaluated against simultaneous obligations to provide energy, FCAS, system strength, and inertia. The binding-resource problem is structurally more central to the current investment portfolio than to the historical one.

Specific time-bound claims: the FCAS-RERT mutual-exclusion under NER 3.20.3(j)<sup>12,51</sup> was salient in 2017–2018 and may have been moderated by subsequent market reforms. The dynamic-tariff design trade-offs<sup>10,11,60</sup> are actively being resolved in Project Edith and DEIP processes through 2024–2026. The kinetic-thermodynamic trade-offs in ammonia and DRI chemistry are time-invariant.

## 7. Mitigation Patterns

Mitigations observed in the corpus fall into four categories.

*Move the trade-off to a different resource.* Adding a battery alongside a wind farm transfers the FCAS headroom problem from the wind farm's available power to the battery's reserved capacity — solving the wind farm's curtailment problem at the cost of adding new capital. Oversizing GFM inverters at Liddell to 86% operating capacity converts a real-time trade-off into a capex trade-off<sup>19</sup>. These mitigations are effective when the moved-to resource is cheaper than the original; they fail when capital cost erodes the business case.

*Accept the trade-off and price it.* Hornsdale 2's PPA provider absorbed the financial impact of FCAS curtailment because the impacts were small enough given the trial circumstances<sup>67</sup>. Reactive-power prioritisation can be enabled or disabled as a matter of grid-code negotiation rather than design<sup>45</sup>. This mitigation is effective when the counterparty has flexibility; it fails when contracts are rigid.

*Co-optimise across the frontier.* AEMO's MASS verification framework, Lake Bonney's later optimisation modules<sup>66</sup>, and bid-stacking algorithms in V2G all attempt to find the operating point on the trade-off frontier that maximises total value. This requires accurate forecasts, which themselves face a forecast-skill ceiling<sup>23</sup>. The combination — coupled-objective trade-off plus forecast uncertainty — is harder to manage than either alone.

*Invest in better resources.* Synthetic inertia with VMM partially decouples inertia from energy headroom<sup>3</sup>. Tandem-cell research aims to widen the photon-allocation frontier through better band engineering<sup>24,25</sup>. Process intensification in ammonia synthesis (membrane reactors) shifts the equilibrium-rate frontier<sup>33,68</sup>. These are R&D-grade mitigations whose payoff is structural but slow.

The general lesson is that mitigation effectiveness is sub-pattern-specific. Headroom trade-offs respond well to capital additions; chemistry trade-offs respond only to fundamental research; market-architectural trade-offs respond to rule reform; design trade-offs around comprehensibility require iterative co-design.

## 8. Implications for Portfolio Decisions

A portfolio manager who recognises this archetype as pervasive should change three decision points.

*At funding.* Business cases should be required to identify the binding resource that two or more project objectives share, and to estimate the slope of the trade-off frontier at the proposed operating point. A project that proposes to deliver simultaneous FCAS and energy revenue, or simultaneous inertia and energy arbitrage, or simultaneous high efficiency and high stability in a tandem cell, should present a co-optimisation analysis rather than two separate revenue projections. Hornsdale's net trial loss of approximately $59,000 (FCAS revenue minus curtailed energy value)<sup>13</sup> is a forecastable outcome from the headroom mechanics alone, not a surprising result.

*At milestone review.* When a project reports underperformance against a single metric, the review should ask whether the metric is one side of a coupled trade-off whose other side is being delivered. Lake Bonney's energy arbitrage shortfall<sup>15</sup>, ESCRI-SA's similar shortfall<sup>69</sup>, and several FCAS trial losses are not failures against a complete metric set; they are predictable expressions of the headroom trade-off. Reviewing both metrics together changes the assessment.

*At knowledge sharing.* The corpus contains substantial overlap in how different projects rediscover the same shape of trade-off. A coordinated knowledge product on the binding-resource analysis pattern — what the resource is, how to estimate the frontier slope, when capital additions move the trade-off versus eliminate it — would prevent the third and fourth project in a category from spending discovery effort on a known structure. The Hornsdale-2, Musselroe, Lake Bonney and ESCRI experiences in 2017–2021 collectively converged on a small set of conclusions that could have been transferred forward to GFM battery projects in 2022–2025 with less duplicated effort.

For the time-variant sub-patterns specifically, the portfolio should acknowledge that older evidence may no longer reflect current rule sets. The FCAS-RERT mutual-exclusion of 2017–2018 may not bind today; the NER reactive-current limits cited at HPRX in 2019 may be different now. Where a current project's business case rests on a regulatory state that has since shifted, due diligence should include current-rule confirmation rather than reliance on the older record.

## 9. Open Questions and Evidence Gaps

Several sub-patterns are thinly evidenced and warrant attention.

The customer-trust trade-off in DOE-style schemes<sup>62</sup> rests on only four records. As DOEs roll out at scale through 2026 and beyond, evidence will accumulate quickly, but the corpus today does not establish whether the simplification-vs-accuracy frontier is steep or shallow in customer perception, and so does not determine which side of the frontier projects should default to.

The geothermal coupled-objective trade-off<sup>70,71</sup> has only three records, all from a now-closed project corpus. The corpus does not tell us whether geothermal trade-offs (permeability vs short-circuiting; reduction vs HER selectivity) generalise to other deep-resource settings.

The electrolyser-grid-connection trade-off<sup>72,73</sup> — between behind-the-meter DC-to-DC efficiency and direct-grid capacity factor — was identified as unresolved at the close of two hydrogen projects. Whether subsequent FEED studies (e.g. CQ-H2, Gibson Island, Lochard) have resolved this is not visible in the corpus.

More generally, the corpus rarely provides the *quantitative slope* of the trade-off frontiers it documents. We know that FCAS headroom requires curtailment, but the dollar-cost of one MWh of energy foregone per MW-hour of FCAS provided varies by project, market state, and time of day, and is often calculated post-hoc rather than in design. Asking projects to surface this slope explicitly, both pre-commitment and post-operation, would substantially improve the portfolio's ability to anticipate where the next coupled-objective trade-off will bind.

A final gap: the corpus contains few records where the trade-off was anticipated, characterised, and successfully navigated. The visible cases tend to be those where the trade-off bound harder than expected. There is likely a selection bias in knowledge-sharing reports toward post-hoc trade-off recognition rather than ex-ante design; deliberate solicitation of "trade-off characterisation" deliverables in milestone reporting would help close this gap.

## [T3] pipeline/development/arena_closure/output/project_reports/neoen_big_battery_western_downs_deployment_project_report.md

# Neoen Big Battery (Western Downs) — Portfolio-Review Synthesis

## 1. Framing

The Western Downs Battery Energy Storage System (WDBESS) is a 200 MW / 400 MWh grid-scale battery in southern Queensland, supported by $21m of ARENA funding within a $243.88m total project value under the Advancing Renewables Program. It sits in ARENA's Large-Scale Battery Storage (LSBS) cohort — the funding round explicitly targeting the deployment of advanced (grid-forming, GFM) inverter capability at scale on the NEM. WDBESS's role in the portfolio is therefore not "another battery"; it is one of a handful of first-of-kind GFM deployments whose lessons are being mined to retire industry risk for the much larger pipeline behind it.

The evidence base spans 136 project records across 31 mechanism clusters and 20 parent archetypes, drawn from three publicly released documents: a Development Report (Milestone 2) published December 2024, Lessons Learnt Report 2 (February 2025), and Lessons Learnt Report 3 (January 2026). All records nominally carry project year 2023, but they describe a window stretching from the 2023 funding-and-procurement decisions through the 5.3.9 grid connection negotiation and Hold Point 1 testing in 2024–2025. The records cover the development, connection-application and early-commissioning stages — they do not yet cover steady-state operations.

## 2. The mechanism-family map

The footprint is heavily concentrated in regulatory, market-design and inverter-grid-interaction families. Five parent archetypes account for the bulk of what bit this project.

**Regulatory novelty and framework misfit (p23, p25, p26, p41).** This is the dominant story. The NER, the connection process, and the FCAS market specifications were all designed around grid-following (GFL) inverter behaviour, and WDBESS hit the seams when those instruments had to accommodate GFM. In [c903] the project absorbed a direct revenue hit when NER v218 (December 2024) broadened the definition of inertia to include synthetic contributions, which AEMO then used to reduce the Very Fast FCAS enablement registered for WDBESS during the 5.3.9 transition<sup>1,2,3,4</sup>. The change landed *after* the project had committed and was already underway, so the FCAS revenue forecast at financial close no longer holds<sup>2</sup>. In [c682] the project flags that the magnitude of the hit is still unknown, because AEMO has not finalised its synthetic-inertia treatment<sup>5</sup>. In [c874] the same regulatory immaturity manifested as a post-registration s5.3.9 process: AEMO and Powerlink could not assess GFM 1-second FCAS contributions cleanly and reached an interim arrangement to register 5 MW below the calculated value, with the door left open to revisit<sup>6,7</sup>. In [c679] the s5.3.4A(b)(1A) "no less onerous" rule turned into a backwards-looking constraint, because GFM reactive settling times are longer than the GFL baseline being used as the floor<sup>8</sup>. And in [c007] the standard architecture pushes frequency control through the Power Plant Controller rather than natively at the inverter terminals, imposing a communications delay that capable hardware cannot otherwise overcome<sup>9</sup>.

**Value capture blocked by market structure (p22).** Three records in [c739] make the point that there is no NEM market that prices GFM services or synthetic inertia, so grant funding (rather than revenue) had to do the heavy lifting at FID<sup>10,11,12</sup>. [c942] adds the corollary: the System Strength Charge avoidance was only realised because the SSC rule change post-dated WDBESS's commitment, so the GFM premium is hard to justify on its own merits going forward<sup>13</sup>.

**Inverter-based-resource grid-interaction failure (p15).** Five clusters here, four of them harmonic-flavoured. The dominant narrative is that switching from GFL to GFM altered the WDBESS harmonic emission profile [c1019], and this collided with a concurrent change in Powerlink's harmonic assessment methodology and updated allocations and polygon data, producing a potential exceedance at the 14th harmonic<sup>14,15,16</sup>. The downstream consequences cascade: [c1053] flags that future projects should design in harmonic filter contingencies, because the GFL→GFM transition can trigger a need for filtering<sup>17,18</sup>; [c559] notes the exceedance risk is not static — neighbouring connections can shift the resonance picture<sup>19</sup>; [c612] surfaces that the faster GFM control loop changes fault-current behaviour, requiring redesign of protection and arc-flash settings within the BoP<sup>20</sup>; and [c740] frames protection redesign as one of the headline time/effort sinks for the project<sup>21</sup>. [c788] adds the upstream geographic story: the Available Fault Level at the Western Downs node is forecast to fall to zero in the short term as planned VRE crowds in, even though no formal system-strength shortfall has been declared<sup>22</sup>.

**Process and planning friction (p24, p27, p36, p38).** The connection process generated iterative rework [c681]: Tesla updated GFM harmonic data in late 2023; Powerlink released a new IBR power-quality methodology in January 2024; new harmonic allocations and polygon data arrived in August 2024 — three months *into* the 5.3.9 studies — forcing rebase<sup>23,24</sup>. The opacity of the NSP allocation process makes early defensive scoping impossible<sup>24</sup>. [c500] and [c1053] therefore land on the same recommendation: reserve site footprint, electrical design margin and budget for a harmonic filter even if not initially required<sup>25,18</sup>. The asymmetry between the GFL stage 1 (no filter needed) and the GFM transition (filter possible) is a textbook [c645] sequential revelation: resolving the primary GFL design hid the GFM-specific failure mode<sup>26,27</sup>. [c779] and [c1081] capture the procurement coupling: in the Australian BESS market EPC contractors typically bring their own PPC/BMS, so the connection package cannot be finalised until the EPC is selected, which serialises rather than parallelises the critical path<sup>28,29</sup>.

**Knowledge gaps and OEM opacity (p05).** [c536] reads as the optimistic side: AEMO/NSP familiarity with GFM models is expected to improve as more LSBS projects come through, easing future timelines<sup>30</sup>. [c022] is the pessimistic side: PSS/E and PSCAD model capability and compliance with the Power System Model Guidelines remain weak points whenever a new GFM model first hits 5.3.4/5.3.9<sup>31</sup>.

Other parents (p06 cycling cost of synthetic inertia<sup>32</sup>; p07 retrofit space exhaustion<sup>33,34</sup>; p11 GFM tuning complexity<sup>35</sup>; p17 OEM-by-OEM heterogeneity in synthetic inertia<sup>36</sup>; p20 GFM capex premium<sup>37</sup>; p39 long-lead harmonic filter<sup>38</sup>; p48 QLD inertia deficit<sup>39</sup>; p49 neighbour-driven study refresh<sup>40</sup>; p01 NSP data inaccessibility<sup>41</sup>) each show up once but support the wider narrative.

## 3. Within-tech reference class

**[c1019] Harmonic profile changes with operational mode.** WDBESS is the canonical GFL→GFM-transition case in this cluster. The Origin Mortlake peer (Battery storage) makes the same systemic argument that filter-driven cost and schedule could decelerate the transition<sup>42</sup>; the University of Wollongong harmonic study confirms the methodological problem (allocation conservatism, summation-law misfit) at theoretical level. The Ekistica grid-forming portfolio synthesis explicitly cites WDBESS as the worked example of the GFL-to-GFM filter problem. Manifestation here is *typical for first-of-kind GFM batteries* but more acute than for GFL-only peers, which were not exposed to the operational-mode-shift dimension.

**[c874] Post-registration s5.3.9 for GFM ambiguity.** The closest peer is AGL Broken Hill — five records describe an essentially identical pattern: voluntary GFM specifications imposed at registration, post-registration s5.3.9 negotiation about voltage-source bandwidth and angle realignment timeframes. Darlington Point shows the same dynamic in NSW. WDBESS's experience is therefore *the modal LSBS-cohort experience*, not an outlier — the cohort is collectively absorbing the cost of NER incompleteness for GFM.

**[c903] Rule change reducing existing project value.** This is a recurring NEM pattern: Lake Bonney was hit by the PFR mandate and PFR Incentive Arrangements transition; Gannawarra was hit by ESS scheduling classification; ESCRI by 5MS; Hornsdale by FCAS constraint relaxation post-system-separation. WDBESS's instance — synthetic-inertia counted against FCAS enablement — is novel in form but *typical in pattern*: the regulatory floor moved during the project's commitment window.

**[c739] Absent market for advanced services.** Highly typical for the LSBS cohort. ESCRI, Hornsdale Power Reserve Upgrade, Wallgrove and Mortlake all flag the absence of paid markets for inertia, system strength or advanced inverter services. WDBESS is consistent with the peer pattern; the persistent gap is the cohort-level signal, not project-specific.

**[c681] Connection requirement uncertainty.** Lake Bonney, Gannawarra and ESCRI all logged this same friction during their connection processes (FSSIA introduction, system-strength assessment changes, NSP iterations). The WDBESS variant is distinctive in that the iteration came from harmonic methodology and allocation updates *during* studies — a tighter, more procedural variant than the more architectural reworks at earlier batteries.

**[c612] GFM fault contribution and arc flash.** Direct alignment with Neoen Victorian Big Battery (Moorabool) and Neoen Blyth — both Neoen sister projects flag the same GFM fault-contribution effect, and both initially scoped on the assumption that no hardware change would be needed. WDBESS is a third instance of the same Neoen-portfolio learning. Cluster signal is now strong enough that it should be a default scoping assumption for any GFM (retrofit or greenfield) project.

**[c1001] GFM tuning complexity.** Strong peer alignment with AGL Broken Hill, Carwarp, Wallgrove and Darlington Point; this cluster reads as the empirical confirmation that GFM tuning is materially more demanding than GFL.

**[c779]/[c1081] EPC/PPC coupling.** The peer is Neoen Blyth, which flags an identical pattern. This is plausibly a feature of the *current* Australian BESS supply chain rather than a permanent constraint.

**[c554] Retrofit space exhaustion.** The WDBESS variant — no space pre-reserved for a harmonic filter — is structurally similar to the SETuP/Daly River BESS retrofit constraints, but at utility scale. The peer-tech precedent is thin for utility batteries specifically; WDBESS is therefore an early data point for the cohort.

## 4. Cross-cutting observations

The most consequential intersection is **regulatory framework gap × IBR grid-interaction × procurement timing**. The harmonic-filter risk did not arise from a single failure mode: it arose because (i) GFM changes the inverter's harmonic profile, (ii) Powerlink simultaneously revised its assessment methodology and allocations, (iii) the revisions arrived three months into the 5.3.9 studies, (iv) the original site was designed without filter footprint, and (v) the EPC coupling means filter procurement could not be parallelised. None of these alone would have been disabling; their compound is what creates the schedule and capex exposure flagged in [c554], [c1053], [c500] and [c004]<sup>33,17,25,38</sup>.

A second compound is **rule change × revenue forecasting**. The NER v218 inertia redefinition, the still-unresolved AEMO synthetic-inertia treatment, and the absence of a paid inertia market combine to make the GFM revenue side genuinely speculative<sup>1,5,11</sup>. ARENA grant funding is doing the work that the market does not yet do<sup>10,12,13</sup>; if the regulatory interpretation tightens further, the cohort-level case for grant-funded GFM premium has to be re-argued from system-benefit grounds, not from project IRR.

A third is **GFM control behaviour × protection design × arc-flash safety**. The faster GFM control loop changes fault current characteristics, which propagates into protection setting redesign, which propagates into arc-flash incident energy and potentially new hardware (inter-trip schemes, relay reviews), which collides with the assumption — made at WDBESS, VBB and Blyth alike — that GFM is "firmware only"<sup>20,21</sup>. This intersection is now well-evidenced enough across the Neoen portfolio to be a default planning assumption.

## 5. Time trajectory

The records line up cleanly across roughly 18 months of project history. The Development Report (Milestone 2, December 2024) lays out the GFM-deployment risk taxonomy as anticipated risks at the connection-application stage — protection redesign, GFM tuning, market absence, OEM heterogeneity, capex premium<sup>11,12,20,21,31,35,36,37</sup>. Lessons Learnt Report 2 (February 2025) is the operationalised version: the harmonic-filter risk has crystallised as a real exceedance at the 14th harmonic, the NSP data opacity is now framed as a structural problem, and retrofit space is identified as a hard constraint<sup>14,15,16,23,24,33</sup>. Lessons Learnt Report 3 (January 2026) closes the loop on the FCAS revenue side: NER v218, AEMO's synthetic-inertia interpretation, and the post-HP1 registration outcome materialise the revenue downside that earlier reports had flagged as a risk<sup>1,2,3,4,6,32</sup>.

Persistence vs resolution: the **harmonic-filter problem persists** in latent form — design contingencies are the recommended mitigation but the underlying NSP-process opacity is unresolved<sup>24,25</sup>. The **FCAS-revenue impact persists** and deepens — the magnitude is not bounded because AEMO has not landed a final position<sup>5</sup>. The **GFM registration ambiguity persists** but is at least operationally containable through interim arrangements<sup>6</sup>. The **protection/arc-flash issue resolves** via redesign within the BoP — pattern is now well-understood, even if it adds work<sup>20,21</sup>.

## 6. What this implies for analogous future projects

For any portfolio manager assessing the next GFM battery proposal under broadly similar 2024–2026 NEM conditions:

- **Treat GFM as a hardware-and-firmware change, not firmware-only.** The protection-redesign and arc-flash hardware footprint shows up at WDBESS, VBB and Blyth — three Neoen projects, same pattern<sup>20,21</sup>. Greenfield designs should reserve site space and cable-route provision for a harmonic filter even if first-stage studies do not require one<sup>25,33</sup>.
- **Price in registration uncertainty on the FCAS side.** WDBESS's experience with synthetic inertia being counted against Very Fast FCAS enablement<sup>1,3,4,6</sup> is likely to recur until AEMO finalises its synthetic-inertia treatment. Revenue cases that depend materially on Very Fast FCAS should stress-test against AEMO's evolving interpretation rather than a static MASS reading.
- **Sequence the 5.3.9 process around NSP data drops, not around internal milestones.** WDBESS lost three months of study work to a Powerlink allocation/methodology update mid-process<sup>23</sup>; the structural fix (NSP transparency) is outside the proponent's control, but defensive scheduling is not<sup>24</sup>.
- **Be honest about GFM revenue.** The grant component is doing real work that the market does not<sup>10,11,12</sup>. The disappearance of SSC at WDBESS was a timing accident<sup>13</sup>; future projects should not bank on that.
- **EPC/PPC procurement coupling is a critical-path item.** Connection package finalisation and EPC selection are serialised in the current Australian market<sup>28,29</sup>; either accept the schedule consequence or do the work upfront to make inverter-OEM-native PPCs acceptable to EPC contractors.

Time-bound dependencies: every one of these recommendations is conditioned on the NER state circa 2024–2026, the Powerlink IBR methodology of January 2024, AEMO's still-evolving synthetic-inertia interpretation, and the present concentration of EPC supply. As more LSBS projects clear the connection process, [c536]'s familiarity dividend should compress some of these timelines<sup>30</sup>.

## 7. Open questions and evidence gaps

The corpus is rich on connection and pre-commissioning friction but has nothing yet on operational performance. Specific gaps:

- No throughput/efficiency measurement for the synthetic-inertia provision flagged in [c622]<sup>32</sup> — the cycling cost of GFM is asserted, not yet quantified for this asset.
- No quantified FCAS revenue outcome — Lessons Learnt 3 indicates the impact is unknown<sup>5</sup>; an operational report would close this.
- No resolution on whether a harmonic filter actually gets installed — the corpus stops at "potentially required, hard to retrofit"<sup>14,15,33</sup>.
- No data on the Available Fault Level trajectory at the Western Downs node<sup>22</sup> as further VRE commits — relevant for the next QLD GFM connection in this region.
- The peer-tech reference class for utility-scale BESS retrofit space constraints [c554] is thin; whether WDBESS is exceptional or representative is not yet inferable.
- The 93 unclustered residuals (more than two-thirds of the project's records) likely contain operational, financial and stakeholder material that is not surfaced here. A targeted re-extraction once commissioning records are published would materially sharpen the picture.
